intro: Ghisonaccia sits on the eastern plain of Corsica, and it holds two French Tree of the Year winners within a kilometre and a half of each other. The Arburacellu, a cork oak of roughly 200 to 250 years, grew bark outgrowths that read, from the right angle, as a bird of prey; the public voted it tree of the year in 2018. U Listincu is far older, a mastic reckoned at 700 to 1,000 years, rooted in the stonework of a Roman ruin, national winner in 2011. Both stand near the hamlet of Gattone, free to visit.
meta_description: Ghisonaccia's two tree-of-the-year winners: the bird-shaped Arburacellu cork oak and U Listincu, a 700-1,000 year mastic rooted in a Roman ruin.
question_meta: Ghisonaccia's oldest tree is U Listincu, a mastic reckoned at 700 to 1,000 years, rooted in a Roman-era ruin near Gattone.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Ghisonaccia is U Listincu, a mastic tree reckoned at 700 to 1,000 years old, rooted in the stonework of a Roman-era ruin on the Gattone plain south of the village. It won France's national Tree of the Year vote in 2011 and was labelled an Arbre remarquable de France the following year.
question_context: Mastic is normally a shrub. Along most of the Mediterranean it grows waist-high and gets browsed by goats; this one grew into a tree, and it is one of only about fifty ancient lentiscs known across the whole basin. Its age is an estimate rather than a ring count, and no source records a measured circumference, so the range stays wide rather than sharpened. It grows out of a Roman-era ruin on the Gattone plain, its roots worked into the old stonework. France recognised it in 2011, seven years before the cork oak in the next fields over, the Arburacellu, won the same national vote for its bird-shaped bark. The two now sit inside a kilometre and a half of each other, joined by one signed circuit from the village: about two kilometres by bike, four on foot through the orchards. It stands in a fenced enclosure with a gate left open for visitors.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Ghisonaccia?
faq.a: U Listincu, a mastic tree reckoned at 700 to 1,000 years old, rooted in the stonework of a Roman-era ruin on the Gattone plain. It won France's national Tree of the Year vote in 2011.

faq.q: Is U Listincu the same tree as the Arburacellu?
faq.a: No. They are two separate, easily confused trees on the same Gattone plain, less than a kilometre and a half apart. U Listincu is a mastic (lentisc); the Arburacellu is a cork oak shaped like a bird. Both won France's Tree of the Year, seven years apart.

faq.q: How old is U Listincu exactly?
faq.a: Nobody has taken a ring count. The estimate, 700 to 1,000 years, comes from the judges of the 2011 competition. If you have measured its girth, tell us; no source records one.

faq.q: Can I visit both trees in one trip?
faq.a: Yes. A signed circuit from the village links them, roughly two kilometres by bike or four on foot through the orchards, so the pair make one afternoon.

trees.name: The Arburacellu (the Bird Tree)

location.address: Strada di u Listincu, near Gattone, 20240 Ghisonaccia, Haute-Corse, Corsica, France

trees.story:
Two people out picking wild asparagus found this tree in 2017. A year later, France voted it the country's tree of the year.

What they walked into is a cork oak of roughly 200 to 250 years, fifteen metres tall and four metres round, shaped like a bird. Lightning is the likely explanation: a strike disrupts the flow of sap, the cork bark grows back wrong, and here it grew into three outgrowths that from the right angle read as a raptor with its head raised and its wings spread. Fire reached it at some point too. The core is burnt and hollow.

The man who found it, out foraging with his granddaughter, took it to the person who had already had Ghisonaccia's other old tree, a mastic reckoned at a thousand years, officially recognised. The oak was entered in the 2018 Arbre de l'Année, run by Terre Sauvage and the national forestry office, and took the public prize with 3,053 votes of more than 12,000 cast. The following year it came fourth in European Tree of the Year, with 29,140 votes of 311,772.

So it is famous for its shape rather than its age, and famous only since a vote, which is rarer still. It stands beside a rural lane on the eastern Corsican plain near Gattone, and people now drive out specifically to find the angle where the bird appears.
trees.access: Free, beside a rural lane near Gattone, with no gate or ticket; listed by the Corse Orientale tourist office among the sights of the area
trees.transport: Rural Corsican plain, reached by car; nearest town is Ghisonaccia
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its bark, deformed by an old lightning strike into three outgrowths that from the right angle read as a bird with wings spread. It stands beside a rural lane near Gattone, outside Ghisonaccia.

trees.name: U Listincu

location.address: Lieu-dit Gattone, near Ghisonaccia-gare, Haute-Corse, Corsica

trees.story:
Mastic is a shrub. Along most of the Mediterranean it grows waist-high, gets browsed by goats and is known mainly for the resin it bleeds. This one is a tree, reckoned at somewhere between 700 and 1,000 years old, and one of only about fifty ancient lentiscs known across the whole basin.

It grows out of a ruin. The roots have taken hold in the stonework of a Roman-era structure on the Gattone plain, south of the village, and worked their way through it. The age is an estimate rather than a ring count, and no source records a measured circumference, so if you have put a tape around it we would like to hear the number.

France caught up with it in 2011, when it won the national Tree of the Year vote run by Terre Sauvage and the forestry office, and in 2012 it was labelled an Arbre remarquable de France. The cork oak in the next fields over, the Arburacellu, took the same prize seven years later. Two national winners inside a kilometre and a half of each other, on one stretch of eastern Corsican farmland.

It now stands in a fenced enclosure with a gate left open for visitors, reached on a signed route from the village: roughly two kilometres by bike, four on foot through the orchards. The same circuit runs on to the oak, so the pair make one afternoon.
trees.access: Free, publicly accessible: the tree stands in a fenced enclosure with a small visitor gate, reached by a signed route of about 2km by vehicle/bike from the village centre, or about 4km on foot through orchards and fields.
trees.transport: Ghisonaccia-gare (Chemins de fer de la Corse) is the nearest station; the tree is reached from there via the signed path described above, not a short walk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a mastic grown into a tree rather than a shrub, its roots worked into the stonework of a Roman-era ruin, inside a small fenced enclosure. It stands on the Gattone plain south of Ghisonaccia.
